source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται.
pass_a_gloss: The things following must be given back and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy must be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not think that I am considering their allegories now as the gnosis delivers truth, if they show something else, just like the ancient wise men, they indicate something else. But they say that God passes through all of existence, we however call Him only Creator and Creator by word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray, 'He passes through and fills all things because of purity', since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not one principle. Let them know therefore the so-called matter, uncreated and unformed, as it is said by them, and more boldly not said by Plato. And not knowing the most mystical, one truly existing principle, he says in the Timaeus with the same words. Now therefore let our position be as follows: the thing about all things, whether principle or principles or however it seems to them, is not to be said now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to explain the things that seem according to the present method. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', gave them occasions for material substance. For Epicurus, the idea of spontaneity did not follow from what was said, hence vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. And for Aristotle, providence extended up to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and truth reach the clouds'. For the revelation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all creative muse, but also Greek philosophy, were borrowed from barbarian philosophy. For Plato, at the end of his Republic, says with the same words, 'Here indeed wild men, fiery to see, standing, learning the sound, having taken some privately, led them away, but Aridaeus and the others, having bound their hands and feet and head, threw them down and flayed them, and dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphodels'. For the wild men, fiery, want to indicate angels to him, who, having taken the unrighteous, punish them; He who makes, he says, His angels spirits and His servants fire. And it follows for them that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer.

pass_b_english: We must now take up the remaining points and demonstrate more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics, for instance, claim that God is body and spirit in essence, just as they do the soul. You will find all these ideas stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not imagine that I am now treating their allegories as the gnosis delivers truth, as if they reveal one thing while actually signaling another, like those ancient wise men. The Stoics say that God pervades all of existence; we, by contrast, call Him only the Creator, the Maker by His Word. The statement in Wisdom — "He passes through and fills all things because of purity" — led them astray, because they failed to grasp that these words are spoken of the primal Wisdom created by God. They object: "But the philosophers posit matter at the beginning — the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic — not a single principle." Let them then recognize the so-called matter, described by them as unqualified and unformed, and, even more boldly, as non-existent according to Plato. And not knowing the most mystical truth — that there is only one truly existing principle — he speaks in the Timaeus using the very same words. For now, let our position stand thus: the question concerning all things — whether there is one principle, or many, or whatever they suppose — is not to be addressed at present, for no other reason than the difficulty of explaining these apparent matters by the present method of inquiry. Besides, the prophetic word, "the earth was invisible and unformed," supplied them with occasions for the notion of material substance. As for Epicurus, the intrusion of the idea of chance arose because he did not attend to the plain text, and so came vanity of vanities: all things are vanity. Aristotle, for his part, extended providence only as far as the moon, drawing from this psalm: "Lord, in the heavens is your mercy, and your truth reaches to the clouds" (Psalm 36:5). For the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire — the whole creative muse, indeed, but also Greek philosophy — were indebted to barbarian philosophy. Plato, at the end of his Republic, speaks in these very words: "Here indeed wild men, fiery to look upon, stood by, discerning the sound; taking some aside privately, they led them away, but Aridaeus and the others they bound hand and foot and head, threw them down and flayed them, and dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphodels." They claim that these fiery wild men represent angels who, seizing the unrighteous, punish them; "He makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire." And it follows for them that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or disciplined, existing in sensation, lives on, even if it is said to suffer.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex arguments regarding the origins of Greek philosophy and the Stoic/Platonic views on matter and providence. Scripture citations (Psalm 36:5) are correctly identified and added in Pass B. The translation of 'ἄποιον' as 'unqualified' (Pass B) or 'uncreated' (Pass A) is acceptable within the context of discussing the nature of matter. The translation of 'διάπυροι' as 'fiery' is consistent. All clauses are accounted for.
